svg.title: Connect each observation to the claim it can support
svg.desc: Griffith-style transformation shows a heritable change in a living bacterial lineage after exposure to material from heat-killed virulent bacteria, but does not alone identify the chemical agent. Avery and colleagues found DNA destruction removed transforming activity in their controlled assay. Hershey and Chase compared DNA-associated and protein-associated radioactive labels during bacterial infection; DNA label was more closely associated with the infected bacterial fraction than most protein label. For structure, Chargaff’s double-stranded DNA base relationships constrain pairing, Franklin’s X-ray diffraction constrains helical form and dimensions, and Wilkins and others contributed structural evidence. Watson and Crick synthesized chemical and structural constraints into a double-helix model whose copying implication required further tests. No source artwork or radioactive data is fabricated.

g.text: Connect each observation to the claim it can support
Historical experiments and model construction answer related but distinct questions.
Transformation and the identity of hereditary material
Griffith: killed virulent cells + living non-virulent cells can yield a changed living lineage.
Avery and colleagues: destroying DNA removed transforming activity in their assay.
Hershey–Chase: DNA-associated label entered the bacterial fraction more than most protein label.
Independent constraints on a structural model
Chargaff: double-stranded DNA has A ≈ T and G ≈ C, with species-dependent composition.
Franklin: X-ray diffraction constrained helical structure and dimensions; it was not an atom photo.
Wilkins and others contributed structural evidence; chemical measurements also constrained models.
Watson and Crick built a model that had to satisfy the combined chemical and structural evidence.
Complementary strands suggested a copying mechanism that still required experimental testing.
No one experiment supplied the whole structure or proved every possible biological claim.
